Paper:
title: Counting on Dummies: Privacy Amplification with Observable Counts and Truncated Batches
summary: In many practical deployments of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), the server processes data in batches. Randomly sampling these batches allows for better privacy bounds via privacy amplification results. Most sampling schemes with provable privacy amplification, including Poisson sampling and random allocation, result in variable batch sizes. The privacy guarantee of these schemes requires that the batch sizes are not revealed. In distributed settings, the server performing the aggregation or any party observing the communication traffic may learn these batch sizes. Furthermore, in both centralized and distributed settings, memory and computation constraints may require each batch to be of some maximum size $s$, necessitating truncation of the batch when it exceeds this limit. It is known that this truncation can result in a significant increase in privacy loss. In this work, we address both of these challenges via a simple mechanism that uses a random number of \emph{dummy points} to privatize the batch size and maintain the privacy guarantee even under truncation. We demonstrate that our mechanism is easy to implement in a distributed setting, and provide a general analysis of this mechanism for both Poisson sampling and random allocation. Our analysis is designed to support efficient and relatively tight privacy accounting. It also effectively amplifies the privacy of the count releases by subsampling, making the expected number of dummy points asymptotically smaller than what is needed to directly privatize the (sensitivity-one) batch sizes with non-negative noise. For Poisson sampling with truncated batches, we demonstrate empirically that our mechanism achieves better privacy--efficiency tradeoffs than the direct accounting for truncation recently given by (Ganesh, 2025).

Paper:
title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
summary: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

Paper:
title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
summary: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, but did not examine the effects of label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffolds, or existing memories. Following its GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D adjudication, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle and the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a 2x2 factorial experiment, a memory experiment, and control experiments (an unlabeled same-protocol baseline, a one-day interleaved control, and benign tasks). The results show that, under authentic envelopes, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate (-56 to -61 percentage points), and the benefit of weak labels is about a quarter to a half of that of strong labels; forging the envelope weakens the strong label's benefit (interaction OR = 2.10, p = 0.022) and its direction varies across frontends; the effect of memory valence exceeds that of any label manipulation; success memory raises the semantic breach rate and failure memory lowers it, while most conflict combinations return to the no-memory baseline; the interleaved control reproduces the direction that "unlabeled is worst"; and on benign tasks the cost of strong labels appears in layers across frontends and backends. Accordingly, this paper extends the envelope layer into "admission surface plus context assembly surface," whose security boundary is a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.

Paper:
title: Beyond Smart Homes: Characterizing IoT Vulnerabilities Across Sectors, Vendors, and Products
summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) has expanded beyond consumer smart homes to sectors, such as industrial systems, healthcare, and smart cities, broadening the IoT attack surface. Prior empirical work has focused on studying aggregate IoT vulnerability characteristics or specific protocols, so patching is directed by aggregate security guidance. However, if dominant weaknesses differ substantially across sectors or products, such uniform guidance misdirects the remediation effort. To address this gap, we present a fine-grained, data-driven analysis of IoT vulnerabilities using a dataset of more than 15,000 IoT specific CVEs. We design a pipeline to enrich noisy CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) metadata, normalizing vendors and products, then assigning product type and sector labels using lexical matching, fuzzy clustering, and LLM-assisted classification. We find meaningful differences in the weakness profile of IoT sectors. For example, healthcare is dominated by authentication and credential weaknesses, while automotive faces memory issues. More importantly, we find that weakness profiles are more similar across different product types from the same vendor than across the same product type built by different vendors. This suggests vendor-level factors such as shared code and development practices dominate weakness inheritance, making a vendor's disclosure history informative about its other products. Our findings suggest weakness classes should be used to prioritize remediation efforts.

Paper:
title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
summary: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.

Paper:
title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
summary: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly.
  We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent.
  To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities.
  We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

Paper:
title: Model Checking for Metric Extensions of Monadic Second-Order Logic
summary: Monadic second-order logic yields powerful algorithmic meta-theorems, but cannot express that a vertex set induces a shortest path. We study metric extensions of counting monadic second-order logic and identify structural parameters supporting efficient model checking, optimization, and counting.
  We show that shortest paths and equidistance guarded by geodesic cycles are definable in ordinary vertex-set MSO on graph classes of bounded cycle-basis length. This yields fixed-parameter tractable model checking for the corresponding extensions of CMSO2, parameterized by formula length and bag-connected treewidth, and of CMSO1, parameterized by formula length and geodesic cliquewidth: the sum of cliquewidth and cycle-basis length. The translations preserve free variables, yielding additive optimization and counting. Applications include Minimum Geodetic Set and Strong Metric Dimension for geodesic cliquewidth, and Minimum Isometric Path Partition for bag-connected treewidth.
  We also introduce restricted packing-covering templates that allow numerical distance thresholds to remain outside the parameter. For each fixed template, feasibility, additive vertex-weight optimization, and counting are fixed-parameter tractable in bag-connected treewidth. Applications include Distance-r Dominating Set, d-Scattered Set, and Minimum Eccentricity Shortest Path.
  Finally, we characterize bounded bag-connected treewidth and bounded geodesic cliquewidth through monadic dependence for the corresponding guarded logics. Unguarded distance comparisons have stricter structural boundaries: first-order model checking is AW[*]-complete already on uncolored caterpillars, and model checking a fixed existential monadic sentence is NP-complete on this class.

title: SeQUeNCe.DQC: Full-stack Simulation of Distributed Quantum Computing
summary: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects multiple quantum processing units to overcome the scale limits of monolithic hardware. We introduce SeQUeNCe$.$DQC a new top-level module within the SeQUeNCe package that compiles monolithic circuits into topology-aware execution plans and coordinates their execution using SeQUeNCe's existing quantum-network modules and protocols. We validate SeQUeNCe$.$DQC by reproducing a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation and comparing success probabilities with the reported 71% benchmark. We then evaluate how compiler strategy, topology, and memory capacity jointly govern distributed circuit execution time and success rate. In these experiments, our hybrid compilers successfully identified mixed TeleGate/TeleData execution plans that outperformed pure gate-teleportation strategies. By capturing the physical overhead of distributed quantum primitives, SeQUeNCe$.$DQC provides a rigorous platform for co-designing DQC software and hardware architectures.

Paper:
title: TileMaxSim: Roofline Regimes and Compression Limits for Fused GPU MaxSim Scoring
summary: MaxSim scoring dominates the cost of multi-vector retrieval. Several groups built fused GPU kernels for it independently during 2026, and all report one measure of success: the fraction of peak memory bandwidth reached. That measure assumes the operator is limited by the bytes it moves. We show the assumption fails in two ways, and that two other quantities decide performance: which side of the roofline ridge a shape falls on, and how many dependent gathers the scoring path performs. We first locate the boundary. Fused arithmetic intensity is Nq*Nd /(Nq + Nd) FLOP per byte, against an H100 dense-FP16 ridge of 295.4. The operator is therefore memory-bound at ColBERT shapes and compute-bound at ColPali-scale query lengths. Published analyses report one side each and do not reconcile them. We measure the crossover at three document lengths, and a closed form predicts it inside the measured bracket each time. Past the crossover, percent of peak bandwidth falls to 4% while percent of peak FLOPs rises above 40%. The reported measure is therefore defined on only one side of a boundary that real workloads cross. We also validate the underlying traffic model against DRAM counters, to 0.003%. We then show that moving fewer bytes does not make the kernel faster. Fusing product-quantized asymmetric distance computation into the kernel moves 15.9x fewer bytes than exact FP16 on tensor cores and runs 3.0x slower. Counters rule out the usual causes: it reaches 1.23% of peak DRAM throughput at 98.2% occupancy. The limit is 6.5*10^9 dependent gathers, a count that does not fall when the codes get smaller. title: Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching
summary: We study decentralized computation of the player-optimal stable matching (POSM) with unannounced player arrivals and departures. Without a common clock, event information, or direct communication, players propose to arms and observe only their own accept/reject outcomes. title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. Paper:
title: Exploring Bad Minima in Transfer Learning
summary: Transfer learning is a highly successful learning paradigm in deep learning which leverages knowledge from one task and applies it to another. Despite its success, the necessary conditions for knowledge transfer are unclear and require further research. In this dissertation, our aim is to understand transferability a little better by answering the following question: Does good generalization on a source task necessarily imply transferability to a related target task? We hypothesize the answer is negative, and attempt to find counterexamples via adversarial attacks on the transfer learning procedure. Over three types of adversarial attacks, our empirical results show a strong relationship between generalization on the source task and transferability. These results do not rule out generalization on the source task as a sufficient condition for successful transfer.

Paper:
title: What Standard Evaluations Hide About Detectors of Hijacked LLM Agents: Rare Attacks, Unseen Tools and Benchmark Transfer
summary: Detectors can flag hijacked large language model (LLM) agents from the traces of the tools they call. In the eleven evaluations we audited, attacks or anomalies make up 16% to 86% of the test samples, no evaluation varies that share, and six report no test on data from a second benchmark or source. We ask what such evaluations hide. On the AgentDrift and AgentDojo benchmarks we test trained detectors that read tool identities, behavior, call sequences, step embeddings or text, and a released LLM action monitor, AlignmentCheck, with thresholds fixed on training data or set by the monitor's released decision rule. First, at a 2% attack rate a detector with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.879 reaches a precision of 0.076, and the mix of negatives alone moves that precision between 0.039 and 0.117. Second, as tool coverage, the share of test tool calls whose tool was seen in training, falls, detector rankings cross near 50% coverage and reverse below it, because unseen tools map to inputs that training never reached. Dropout on tool inputs largely removes the reversal. Third, no detector trained on AgentDrift ranks AgentDojo traces better than chance (AUROC 0.47 to 0.52), including one that reaches 0.996 within AgentDojo. The monitor, trained on neither, reaches 0.930, but with its open backbone its released decision rule would still mostly raise false alerts at a 2% attack rate (precision 0.096). We turn these findings into a checklist for evaluating trace detectors.

Paper:
title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
summary: Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

Paper:
title: On the Expressiveness of Asynchronous Processes with Nested Session Types (Extended Version)
summary: Session types are a type-based approach to correct message-passing programs, where types specify protocols for channels and type checking guarantees communication correctness. Traditional session types express regular protocols only, which leaves out many protocols found in practice. Aiming at overcoming this limitation, Nested Session Types (NSTs) can specify nested recursive protocols. NSTs are known to be characterised by one-counter machines and deterministic context-free languages. In this paper, we study the expressiveness of ASP (Asynchronous Session Processes), the process model associated with NSTs as introduced by Das et al. We prove that AST is Turing complete by giving a correct encoding of two-counter machines into typed processes. Our encoding uses a non-trivial state-aware representation of counters and instructions that is neatly governed by NSTs.

Paper:
title: Do User-Authored Permission Policies Improve Protection Against AI Agent Overreach?
summary: AI agents are poised to become a primary interface to digital products, acting across email, files, payments, and personal data. People without professional software backgrounds need understandable, reusable ways to control actions across services. We examine a mechanism in which a language model maps actions to plain-language consequence categories with user-authored "allow", "ask", or "never" rules. We ask what is gained and lost when decisions are made in advance as reusable rules rather than separately for each action.
  We analyzed 113 participants without professional software backgrounds across three conditions: per-action human-in-the-loop approval (HITL), automated per-action model review (AUTO), or user-authored consequence policy (POLICY). Participants judged 2 examples in each of 4 consequence categories; POLICY participants then set one rule per category. All supervised an 18-action simulated day, including 7 overreach actions. POLICY blocked less overreach than HITL (-20.1 percentage points, 95% CI [-32.1, -8.1]) and AUTO (-14.5 points, 95% CI [-25.8, -3.2]). POLICY lowered runtime prompts from 18.0 to 10.9, but total intervention time was not reliably lower when rule setup was included.
  Exploratory analysis showed that participants chose "ask" for 114 of 140 POLICY rules, returning most overreach actions to runtime. Of the 148 overreach actions executed in POLICY, 133 followed human approval and 15 ran automatically under "allow" rules. Across all 7 overreach actions, POLICY had the highest approval rate. Counterintuitively, user-authored rules did not by themselves provide stronger protection: many actions outside users' original requests went through after users approved them. These results reveal a gap between preference and commitment: repeatedly choosing "ask" preserves case-by-case choice but prevents a standing policy from settling decisions in advance.

Paper:
title: From Training Exposure to Membership Evidence: A Controlled Study of OLMo 2
summary: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. A reference trained with another seed recovers 92% of the counterfactual's AUC advantage over chance, whereas reference-free attacks stay within 0.07 of chance when pooled over domains. The full official post-training recipe, re-run on both models, leaves 89% of the average effect. Even with a closely matched reference, substantial document-level variability limits individual membership inference. We will release the checkpoints, per-token log-probabilities, and the evaluation documents; the code is available at https://github.com/ali-bana/OLMo-Twin.

title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
summary: AI control relies on monitors to catch a capable model that sabotages its work. These monitors are evaluated on their ability to differentiate honest from backdoored code. We show that on a standard evaluation dataset, simple features beat most monitors without ever running the code, outranking 20 of 24 open-weight models prompted as monitors. The dataset gives its labels away in two ways. People wrote the honest solutions and older language models the backdoors, so the style of the code reveals the class. Additionally, problems that LLMs can backdoor have different characteristics, so basic facts about the problem reveal it too. Swapping one class at a time for code by Claude Sonnet 5 shows that these features reward a contrast between authors, since human code against Sonnet 5's backdoors is easier to separate than the original pairs, 0.95 against 0.79. One in seven backdoors in the standard test set fails our validity checks, which distorts comparisons between attackers. A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified. We do not show that published monitors rely on these shortcuts, but our findings suggest that a high score on such a dataset is not by itself evidence of sabotage detection. We release the rebuilt dataset and checks.

Paper:
title: Fooling Relying Parties of the EUDI Wallet Architecture: Credential Pooling Attacks and CRESTA, a Standard-Compliant Countermeasure
summary: The European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet will let millions of EU citizens prove who they are and what they are entitled to, disclosing only what is needed. Many services need several credentials at once, such as an identity card and a university degree, so combined presentations are essential.
  We present credential pooling attacks on relying parties of the EUDI Wallet reference architecture. Colluding users, each holding some credentials in their own wallet, cooperate through a proxy that acts as a single synthetic user and presents all the requested credentials, although no single user holds them all. Every signature is genuine and computed by certified hardware, and nothing is extracted or forged. We ran the attack against the European Commission's reference implementation, also on two Android phones.
  The attack would fail if all credentials of a user carried the same public key, but colluding relying parties could then link all presentations of that user. For this reason, the Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) requires a fresh key for each credential and recommends batches of single-use copies, each with its own key: precisely what makes pooling possible. One might think that preventing pooling requires giving up unlinkability or adopting non-standard cryptography, such as zero-knowledge proofs.
  We show that this is not the case: we present CRESTA (CREdential STApling), an efficient countermeasure that uses only standard cryptography and credential formats and preserves unlinkability. In CRESTA, an ordinary issuer checks at issuance that a set of keys was generated in the same secure hardware, and certifies it in a binding attestation: a standard credential whose attributes can be selectively disclosed. CRESTA works entirely within the EUDI Wallet framework and costs a relying party one additional signature verification per presentation.

Paper:
title: The Guard That Cried Wolf: How Scary Words Make Agent Guardrails Refuse Legitimate Actions
summary: Agent guardrails are checks that approve or refuse each action before an LLM executes it. Sometimes they refuse requests that are genuinely safe. This over-safety blocks deployment when a guardrail refuses an authorized task. Evaluating over-safety is hard: at the boundary an authorized action resembles an unauthorized one, and the safe-versus-unsafe label is a choice of authorization policy, not fixed by the action alone. We argue it therefore requires a benchmark that does not yet exist, one that maps the decision boundary of an ideal guardrail. Harvesting such a benchmark from real data is impractical: boundary cases are hard to collect, their labels hard to verify. The gap is real, so we construct Cautious Bench, the first benchmark to make over-safety the construct for agent guardrails; it codesigns each sample and its label with a stated authorization policy. A build-time gate re-derives every example to certify it, so each label is a mechanical consequence of the policy rather than an annotator's per-sample verdict, a reference against which researchers can measure real guardrails. The benchmark renders 756 Decidable benign/twin pairs, each under three object-name types (2,268 measured pairs), and 40 Undecidable pairs reported separately. Measuring six guardrails from five designs, we find a name-superstition effect: each over-refuses an authorized action more often under a scary-looking object name than a benign one. Since only the object name varies in the aforementioned contrast experiments, the deviation is the name's doing: the guardrails read the surface label, not the authorization context.

title: Poly Versus Polyval
summary: We revisit the basic construction of polynomial evaluation based hash function, which we call Poly, over binary extension fields over $GF(2^n)$, where $n=64k$ and $k\geq 2$. Unlike GHASH, the NIST standard polynomial evaluation based hash function for $n=128$, Poly does not perform the unnecessary bit reversals of each $n$-bit block, and consequently is faster than GHASH. title: HiState: Hierarchical Prefix Cache Management for Hybrid LLM Serving in Agentic Workloads
summary: Hybrid large language models combine full-attention and recurrent linear layers to reduce inference costs. Prefix caching can further reduce redundant computation across requests, but a recurrent checkpoint cannot recover an earlier state corresponding to a shorter prefix. Existing hybrid prefix caching systems retain checkpoints at selected boundaries to support common reuse patterns in conventional conversations. However, agent workloads modify and revisit earlier contexts, exposing reusable prefixes whose checkpoints were never saved or have already been evicted. A straightforward approach is to retain more checkpoints to reduce recomputation, but their cumulative footprint can displace reusable prefixes from other sessions and cause additional cache misses. To address these problems, we present HiState, a prefix cache management system for hybrid models serving agent workloads. Our key observation is that prefix reuse accesses all matching key-value (KV) entries but only one recurrent checkpoint, regardless of how many checkpoints are retained. This asymmetry allows HiState to retain historical checkpoints on SSD while prioritizing fast memory for KV entries: each hit retrieves only one checkpoint whose size is independent of context length. Within this hierarchy, we propose adaptive interval control to balance checkpoint storage against recomputation, and unified eviction to coordinate checkpoint sparsification with reclamation of stale trajectories. We implement HiState on top of vLLM and evaluate it on two public coding-agent trace datasets and controlled microbenchmarks. On real agent traces, HiState achieves up to 5.73x and 5.44x speedups in p99 TTFT over vLLM-Marconi and SGLang-HiCache, respectively.

title: Kidney Exchange with Dual Donors
summary: Kidney exchange programs enable patients with incompatible living donors to receive transplants by exchanging donors with other patient-donor pairs. Existing models typically assume either that each patient enrolls with a single donor, or that at most one of a patient's multiple alternative donors is selected to donate. summary: Modern recommender models scale sparse representations and dense computation together. title: GESIS Surf: An Open-Source Infrastructure for Privacy-Preserving Longitudinal Web Browsing Data Collection

title: Efficient cross-domain multi-factor authentication
summary: Secure cross-domain authentication is crucial for protecting information exchange across terminals in different security domains. title: OrionLink: Single Sign-On with Oblivious Identity Brokers
summary: Single Sign-On (SSO) is a federated authentication mechanism that improves user experience by enabling access to multiple services, or Relying Parties (RPs), through a single authentication at an Identity Provider (IdP). We further instantiate OrionLink with two new features, preserving broker functionality and deployability. We implemented a prototype of OrionLink within a brokered SSO environment, and experimental evaluation shows that the framework achieves substantial security and privacy improvements with acceptable performance overhead.

title: How Much Reconstruction Does Quantum Machine Learning Need? Late Fusion of Uncoupled Quantum Subcircuits
summary: Circuit cutting lets a large quantum neural network (QNN) run as independent subcircuits on small devices, but rebuilding its outputs by quasiprobability reconstruction carries a classical sampling overhead exponential in the number of cuts. title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
summary: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. title: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum
summary: EIP-7702 introduces a new transaction type that allows Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) on major EVM-compatible chains to delegate execution to arbitrary contract codes temporarily. While enhancing functionality, this mechanism facilitates a novel threat: the \underline{E}IP-7702-Based \underline{E}ther \underline{R}edirection \underline{A}ttack (EERA). In such an attack, a victim is delegated to a malicious sweeper contract, which automatically redirects incoming ETH transfers to an address controlled by the attacker. As a nascent attack paradigm arising from protocol evolution, the underlying mechanisms and security implications of EERA remain systematically unexplored. To bridge this gap, we provide the first formal analysis of the EERA attack model and propose SweeperHunter, a framework that detects these attacks through transaction analysis. By evaluating transactions from the first ten months following the introduction of EIP-7702 on Ethereum mainnet, we have identified 4,668,209 malicious delegations, 20,443 attack transactions and 508 ETH sweeper contracts, forming the first EERA dataset. Finally, we analyze this attack from both attacker and victim perspectives, derive key insights, and propose corresponding mitigation strategies. We reveal the prevalence of EERA, as approximately 70\% of the observed delegations point toward ETH sweeper contracts. Furthermore, we observe a notable lack of effective responses from victims; specifically, over 600,000 accounts failed to revoke or update their malicious delegations promptly, thereby remaining in a state of vulnerability. Our research is expected to facilitate understanding and mitigation of this emerging threat posed by EIP-7702.

summary: Keystroke dynamics constitute a cost-effective behavioral biometric, but their timing features degrade under environmental and hardware variation. Paper:
title: Evaluating Structural and SAT Attack Resilience in Cryptographic Dynamic Logic Locking via Keystream Capping
summary: Untrusted third-party entities throughout the semiconductor supply chain expose proprietary hardware intellectual property to reverse engineering, piracy, and overproduction. While logic locking counters this threat by embedding key-dependent logic, conventional static key-gates remain vulnerable to both oracle-guided SAT attacks and structural removal attacks due to their time-invariant netlist signatures. Dynamic schemes such as STREAMLOCK mitigate oracle attacks by continuously masking signals with cryptographic keystream, achieving near 50\% Hamming distance output corruption under incorrect keys with low hardware overhead. However, confining key-gates to primary outputs leaves internal combinational cones vulnerable to single-tap structural bypasses. This work extends dynamic logic locking by distributing key-gates within internal paths prioritized via fault-propagation analysis. The original and internally-hardened architectures are evaluated against structural removal attacks and a bounded, unrolling-based SAT-style attack across three ISCAS'85 benchmarks. Distributing masking internally raises the uninformed attacker's brute-force search space from 6 candidate node subsets to over $10^{45}$ for the largest benchmark. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals that topological relocation alone does not prevent algebraic key extraction when wide circuits expose numerous keystream bits per clock cycle. To eliminate this leak, a keystream-bit reuse cap is introduced to restrict per-cycle exposure independent of circuit width. Under this constraint, SAT-solver tractability encounters an immediate computational cliff, transitioning sharply from rapid under-constrained solving to timeout thresholds without disclosing the secret key. Integrating fault-aware internal placement with keystream reuse capping delivers joint resilience against structural bypasses and bounded SAT attacks.

title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
summary: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. title: Inadvertent Context Leakage in Language Models
summary: For AI agents to be useful beyond simple chat, they must hold sensitive user context such as calendars, credentials, health records, and financial data. We study whether the mere presence of such secrets in a model's context window introduces hidden correlations into the model's benign outputs, allowing reconstruction even when the model correctly refuses direct extraction. title: Competing Auctions in Intermediated Markets
summary: We analyze competing auctions in intermediated markets, where a seller selects among parallel mechanisms for the sale of a single good, most prominently the relay-and-protocol architecture of proposer-builder separation in Ethereum.
  When the intermediary can enforce single-homing on its bidders, sealed-bid second-price intermediary auctions fully unravel into the sealed first-price principal auction; open bidding-format intermediaries unravel only partially, collapsing into first-price in equilibrium under symmetric latency and sorting fast bidders to the intermediary under asymmetric latency. However, if the seller can credibly commit to not leak bids, it is optimal for them to do so.

title: Characterizing Recoverable Expert-Utilization Signatures in Fine-Tuned Mixture-of-Experts LLMs
summary: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models are increasingly deployed in distributed environments, from federated learning to edge-cloud systems, their architecture harbors an underexplored landscape of security vulnerabilities. summary: Serverless execution of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming important, reflecting their wide societal use. title: A Unified Attack Framework against Statistical Generative Watermarks for Large Language Models
summary: Watermarking has emerged as a key tool for identifying text generated by large language models (LLMs), with current schemes embedding statistical signals into the generation process to enable later detection. Paper:
title: LiHA: Worse is Better for Lightweight Hash-based Source Authentication
summary: The omission of source IP authentication remains a fundamental vulnerability in the Internet. Existing approaches rely on routing plausibility, topology assumptions, per-flow state, or wide deployment. These requirements have kept strong source authentication out of the data plane.
  As simplicity is the key to deployability, we present LiHA, a lightweight source authentication mechanism built around operations that routers already perform efficiently. LiHA binds secret keys to source prefixes using longest prefix match and authenticates each packet with a single message authentication code (MAC). The data plane requires no handshakes, per-flow state, or per-packet control plane access. A sender performs one prefix lookup and one fixed-size hash. The verifier repeats the same operations and forwards the packet only if the MAC matches.
  LiHA is designed for incremental deployment. It primarily protects against off-path attackers that spoof source prefixes they do not control. An on-path attacker can replay valid authenticated packets until the key rotates. LiHA does not eliminate every denial-of-service threat. Instead, it confines accepted traffic to authenticated source prefix space within participating networks. We argue that simpler source authentication with clear limits is more likely to be deployed.
  We implemented LiHA in three environments: as a set of user-space libraries, as eBPF programs, and in an FPGA. We found that the user-space implementation had very high overheads. The eBPF implementation got reasonable single thread performance even with a software based cryptographic hash. We found that only the FPGA could obtain 100 Gbps single thread performance, but that was only when bypassing the kernel using a DPDK user-level networking stack.

title: STRIATUM-CTF: A Protocol-Driven Agentic Framework for Autonomous CTF Solving
summary: Autonomous cyber operations increasingly depend on agents that can chain reconnaissance, exploitation, and analysis across many tools while maintaining state over long task horizons. Large Language Models (LLMs) are promising orchestrators for this workflow, but naive agents that pipe model output directly into a shell are brittle: they emit malformed commands, hallucinate non-existent command-line options or packages, and lose track of earlier findings as the context window fills. We present STRIATUM-CTF, a modular agentic framework for Capture-the-Flag (CTF) solving that mediates between LLM reasoning and tool execution using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Offensive-security tools are exposed as strictly typed, schema-validated functions; the protocol layer rejects out-of-schema tool calls before execution and returns structured observations that the agent uses to self-correct. We evaluate the system in two ways. In a controlled study of 180 runs across 15 CTF challenges under four levels of attached procedural documentation, the system succeeds on 77.8-86.7% of attempts; notably, a schema-only configuration with no procedural documentation already reaches 77.8%, and no condition differs significantly from another. In a single live, multi-team CTF at Florida State University, the system placed first against a field of more than 30 registered teams -- a single, non-replicated event decided by a 10-point margin over the runner-up, and therefore a demonstration of feasibility rather than of superiority over human experts. Because all four ablation conditions share the same tool layer, our controlled study isolates documentation volume rather than the protocol layer itself; we accordingly present schema-mediated grounding as a design principle with qualitative support rather than as a measured effect.

Paper: title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities summary: Fil-C retrofits spatial and temporal memory safety onto C/C++ using software capabilities (bounds that are checked at every pointer dereference). Fil-C's guarantee rests on an unstated hardware assumption: that DRAM preserves the capabilities. We show that Rowhammer breaks it. In Fil-C 0.679 a part of each heap pointer's capability lives in a 16-byte header stored inline in ordinary DRAM immediately before the object pointed to, with no mechanism to prevent capabilities from corruption. A single 0 → 1 bit flip in the capability's upper-bound expands the pointer's permitted range by 2k bytes and is invisible to the runtime, raising no panic or signal. We demonstrate this by using Fil-C to convert existing Rowhammer attacks into concrete attacks against a heterogeneous collection of victim software. To aid reproducibility (not everybody has DRAM vulnerable to Rowhammer) we split our demonstration into two paths. First, along a deterministic path, we isolate Fil-C as a novel attack vector using a deterministic, Rowhammer-like fault-injection model. Across four case studies, this model corrupts the upper-bound word of a pointer, permitting previously out-of-bounds reads and writes. We use this to achieve a bounded read/write window, secret disclosure, privilege escalation by flipping an adjacent is_admin field, and the leakage of a tenant API key in a multi-tenant credential service backed by SQLite (compiled under Fil-C). Second, along a physical end-to-end path, we demonstrate all four attacks on real hardware equipped with DDR3 memory, and with Target Row Refresh (TRR) equipped DDR4, proving the exploits are physically realisable. The latter attack shows that the TRR defence does not close the Fil-C delivery channel. We close with a discussion of Fil-C-specific mitigations. link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33748v2
